An estimation of the effective lifetime for the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay mode was obtained using data collected by the LHCb experiment at the LHC, encompassing both $B^0_s$ meson and its antiparticle, with a significance of 10.4 sigma. This analysis involved reconstructing $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay events, with a focus on the displacement between the production and decay points of the particles. A sideband subtraction technique was applied to non-$B^0_s$ events, and a likelihood fit was used to fit the distribution of decay lengths, yielding an effective lifetime of 1.49 ps with an uncertainty of 0.047 ps. This value was derived from statistical and systematic sources of uncertainty.

This research paper examines the numerical solution to a regulation problem in the context of a stochastic option pricing model, represented by a random partial differential equation. The problem involves determining a stopping time and a control variable to minimize expected financial losses, which include option price deviations, startup costs, and stopping and option purchase costs. A non-iterative numerical approach is developed to address this variational inequality problem, and its convergence properties are analyzed, showing that sequences of stopping times and control variables converge to optimal values. Additionally, the paper presents computational results to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.

The Pierre Auger Observatory has recorded the most energetic cosmic rays, providing a crucial dataset for understanding the behavior of ultra-high-energy particles. The analysis of the anisotropy in the directions from which these particles arrive reveals that their arrival directions are not uniformly distributed. At the highest energies, where the anisotropy is most pronounced, the data indicates a correlation with the direction of the Large Magellanic Cloud. To further investigate the anisotropy, researchers have developed a statistical model based on the anharmonic expansion of spherical harmonics. The results of this study are consistent with previous findings and provide a comprehensive picture of the anisotropy in the arrival directions of the most energetic cosmic rays.

This research paper proves that all Zinbiel algebras possess a solvable derived series, indicating their overall solvability. Additionally, it establishes the following properties: Zinbiel algebras contain a derived series with twelve layers, and their derived second algebra is a Lie nilpotent algebra with a specific composition involving their filiform derived second algebra and lower central series. The paper also explores the connection between Zinbiel algebras and a particular subclass of Vinberg algebras, demonstrating that their derived second algebra has a solvable derived series with twelve layers.

A study of the average flow angle fluctuation in lead-lead collisions at the LHC, conducted using 7800 collisions at a centrality-dependent transverse momentum range of 2-6 GeV/c, reveals that the LHC heavy ion collaboration's data on the scaled variance of the signed event plane angle, scaled pT, and average transverse momentum fluctuation show strong correlations. The fluctuations in these variables are found to increase with the decrease in average pT, and they are used to estimate the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio, yielding values of 0.08 to 0.12, 0.09 to 0.12, and 0.08 to 0.12, respectively. The study also provides the first measurement of the magnitude fluctuation in the LHC energy range, yielding a scaled variance of 0.1 to 0.2 across different particle pT ranges and centralities.

A key challenge in data integration is handling inconsistencies that arise when combining data from multiple sources. Traditional research has primarily focused on identifying and resolving conflicts resulting from explicit contradictions, such as incompatible values in the same data field. However, inconsistencies can also stem from violations of fundamental relationships between data fields, known as functional dependencies. These are often implicit and can be easily overlooked. This study delves into data integration problems by examining the interplay between missing data and these implicit inconsistencies. It defines a novel concept called a "hole," to represent a group of interconnected inconsistencies within a table, and develops an algorithm to automatically detect and address these issues. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through its application to a real-world dataset.

We introduce a novel regression method called Time-Dependent Poisson Autoregression (TDARP) to address dynamic generalized linear models with time-varying link functions. TDARP extends traditional GLMs by incorporating a flexible parametric approach to model the time-dependent link function using a polynomial basis, while employing a Poisson likelihood for non-negative response variables. This flexible framework enables TDARP to effectively capture complex, nonlinear relationships between predictors and the response variable in time series data. We derive theoretical properties of the TDARP estimator and establish its asymptotic normality, and further develop a robust covariance estimator to account for potential autocorrelation in the data. Through Monte Carlo simulations and real-world analysis of New York City's taxi trip data, we demonstrate the TDARP model's superior predictive performance compared to standard GLM and time series regression approaches.

Representing individual objects in a scene is a key step for enabling robots to navigate and interact effectively within complex environments. Currently, point cloud-based object representations are prevalent, yet they pose challenges when dealing with partially observed objects. In this work, we introduce a novel object representation called Neural Descriptor Fields (NDF), which is a compact, continuous, and rotationally invariant descriptor field that can be easily integrated into downstream tasks. NDFs are trained using a straightforward, end-to-end approach with a rotation augmentation technique, and they outperform existing methods in multiple tasks, including object recognition, pose estimation, and pose generalization, as well as in a downstream task involving the joint inference of multiple objects in a scene. Our results demonstrate the versatility of NDFs in handling various downstream tasks.

Researchers have determined the precise position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity across O(N) universality classes in two dimensions by applying the functional renormalization group method. A reliable estimate of this position has been established for 26 different classic Yang-Mills theories, revealing a distinct pattern when organized according to their central charges. Notably, the results for supersymmetric theories show alignment with previously derived predictions. Furthermore, the findings have significant implications for the critical behavior of theories in finite spaces and the statistical properties of polymers near their critical point.

In this work, we establish a lemma that extends the comparison technique developed by Montanari and Vegni, which they claim is applicable to a wide range of scenarios, including the analysis of the AMP algorithm's behavior near the spin glass transition. This lemma essentially states that if sequences of random variables, denoted as $\xi_n$ and $\eta_n$, satisfy certain conditions, then the expected value of the difference between two loss functions, $l_n(\eta_n)$ and $l_n(\xi_n))$, is non-negative. Building on this lemma, we provide an alternative proof demonstrating the local convexity of the TAP free energy with respect to the magnetization in the vicinity of the spin glass transition.

Recent research has utilized photometric data from stars to accurately track the vertical distribution of aerosols in the atmosphere. By applying ordinary least squares regression to analyze variations in star brightness over time, researchers can determine the aerosol optical depth (AOD). This method has been successfully applied to calculate AOD values from multiple observatories around the world, including those located in the southern hemisphere. Furthermore, this study develops an enhanced mathematical model to calculate AOD values from the Airmass-Brightness (AB) diagram, which yields more precise results than the traditional method. The improved model takes into account the varying brightness of individual stars and the curvature of the Earth, which can have a significant impact on observed brightness, especially for stars located near the horizon. The research reveals that ignoring these factors can lead to errors in AOD calculations, which can be as high as 0.14. Overall, this study provides a more precise method for monitoring the presence of aerosols in the atmosphere using photometric data from stars.

To accurately estimate the complete six-degree-of-freedom pose of an object, it's essential to determine the object's position and orientation in 2D space, as well as its position along its vertical axis. To address this challenge, we developed a novel approach that involves two main components. Firstly, we introduced a refined network for projecting heatmaps, which handles both 2D and depth maps simultaneously to estimate the object's position. Secondly, we designed a correspondence learning network that leverages the relationships between 2D and depth maps to predict the object's remaining two dimensions of pose. Through extensive testing on multiple datasets, our method outperformed existing techniques in terms of accuracy.

UFLasso, or Graphical Lasso, is a method used to estimate the structure of undirected graphs by analyzing the conditional dependencies between random variables. Researchers have developed a generalized version of the algorithm, known as UGraphLasso, which accommodates graphs with directed and hierarchical relationships. The new Python package, GGLasso, provides access to the UGraphLasso solver and includes additional tools for visualizing results from this analysis.

A new method called the Sequential Configurational Molecular Sampling (SCMS) algorithm is introduced to address the challenge of generating robust and efficient configurations for molecules. This algorithm builds on the existing Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR) technique by incorporating an adaptive strategy for determining the optimal relaxation parameter, which is calculated automatically based on the specific molecule being analyzed. The SCMS algorithm is found to converge rapidly for most molecules, often requiring only a few iterations to reach the desired level of accuracy. The proposed method is particularly effective for large molecules and polymers, where it outperforms the standard integration of the Langevin Dynamics equations in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The SCMS algorithm is also computationally efficient, as it has a low computational cost and can be easily parallelized. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the SCMS algorithm through a range of numerical experiments, including the simulation of a 100,000-bead polymer chain, where it achieves a level of accuracy comparable to that of the standard integration method but at a fraction of the computational cost.

Understanding how to measure the significance of nodes in complex multi-layered networks is crucial for uncovering their underlying structure and behavior. In these networks, which consist of interconnected sub-networks, the relationships between layers can significantly impact the precision of traditional centrality measures. To better assess the connectivity of individual nodes, we have developed a centrality measure that takes into account the connections between network layers, specifically focusing on how nodes are interconnected across different network strata. We have examined our measure's performance across various types of interconnected networks, including those with independent, mutually exclusive, and symmetric relationships between layers, and found that it effectively captures the underlying structure of the networks. We have also demonstrated the applicability of our measure in identifying the most significant nodes in networks that have been affected by attacks or in biological networks, highlighting its potential utility in a wide range of practical scenarios.

In this study, we reformulated the Schrödinger equation with a relativistic energy operator in $R$-Minkowski space-time, and successfully derived Dirac's equation. We then interpreted the resulting $R$-Dirac equation and its equation of motion for the associated spinor field.

This study investigates the behavior of spheres entering water at moderate speeds, specifically between 1.5 and 3 meters per second. During this process, a pocket of air gets trapped beneath the sphere as it submerges. The spheres used in the research varied in surface texture, including smooth, rough, and grooved surfaces. The size of the air pocket was measured and compared to the spheres' diameter and the depth of water entry. The results indicate that smooth-surfaced spheres produce the smallest air pockets, whereas rough and grooved-surfaced spheres generate larger pockets. A dimensionless number, known as the Weber number, is used to describe the relationship between the air pocket size and the sphere's diameter. The research reveals that surface texture significantly affects the size of the air pocket, with smooth surfaces resulting in smaller pockets and textured surfaces leading to larger pockets.

We investigate the low-energy dynamics of global symmetries in Type IIB effective field theories, focusing on axion-dilaton moduli and the associated generalized theta-terms. By analyzing the symmetries of the generalized theta-terms, we determine the possible forms of periodic potentials that preserve these global symmetries. We then construct the most general periodic potential respecting these symmetries and a specific symmetry-breaking pattern, leading to spontaneous breaking of global symmetries and generation of non-zero vacuum expectation values for the $R\wedge R$ and $R\wedge {\rm Im}(\mathcal{F})$ generalized theta-terms. We also explore the implications of this scenario for the cosmological constant and gravitational waves.

The transition from a paramagnetic to a ferromagnetic state in cubanite CuFe2S3 is examined through temperature-dependent, high-resolution X-ray absorption spectroscopy, performed at the Fe L2,3 absorption edges. Our investigation reveals that the iron 3d orbitals in cubanite exhibit significant orbital asymmetry, with the t2g and eg levels showing distinct occupancies and broadening effects that are linked to strong electron correlations and structural distortions. The observed shift in the t2g and eg peaks during the transition from the Curie temperature to the ferromagnetic state indicates a reduction in the net magnetic moment of the iron ions. Our findings are corroborated by theoretical calculations utilizing the DMFT+LDA approach, which provide a comprehensive understanding of the orbital dynamics in cubanite.

The interaction between excitons in semiconducting materials and laser light can lead to a significant drop in transmission, a phenomenon known as the giant Rabi effect. This effect is typically observed in experiments involving semiconductors and requires a magnetic field to occur. A theoretical model has been developed that replicates the giant Rabi effect without the presence of an external magnetic field. This model uses dark excitons with a short lifetime and a high magnetic moment to produce a large fluctuation in transmission. A simulation of the theoretical model matches the actual data obtained from an experiment on gallium arsenide quantum wells, a material that contains dark excitons with a short lifetime.

Our research focuses on a two-dimensional electron-beam lithography network lattice with non-symmorphic symmetry, demonstrating its potential to exhibit Dirac points through its unique symmetry properties. By leveraging the effects of spatial inversion and beam inversion symmetries, we show that this network lattice adheres to time-reversal and spatial inversion invariance, resulting in linear energy dispersion near the high-symmetry $\Gamma$ point in the Brillouin zone. Furthermore, we found that tuning the beam inversion parameters can influence the vanishing of mass terms, allowing for the elimination of an initially parabolic dispersion and the emergence of linear dispersion at the $\Gamma$ point. Our findings have significant implications for the study of non-trivial topological phases and linear topological phases within this network lattice.

Quantum phase distributions of single photons are typically undefined due to the single-particle nature of the electromagnetic field, yet they hold significant potential for advancing quantum technologies. This research proposes an innovative method to create a well-defined single-photon phase distribution by utilizing quantum-optical catalysis to generate a periodic catalyzed photon with a specific wavelength and direction. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations reveal that the process results in a photon's quantum state being described by a single particle with a precise, periodic phase, which can be utilized in cutting-edge quantum applications.

In General Relativity, using the formalism developed by Penrose and others, we explain the detailed structure of bispinors and bivectors, along with their connection to complex vector bases. This understanding forms the foundation for the components of the electromagnetic field and gravitational field in the Newman-Penrose formalism. Specifically, we examine how the components of the electromagnetic field tensor and the Riemann curvature tensor are represented in terms of vector basis components. This analysis reveals that the four components of the latter correspond to the two independent components of the Weyl curvature tensor. This relationship is further illustrated through the analysis of gravitational plane waves in vacuum.

This research combines linear regression and integer programming to create a method for determining the molecular formula of polymers. By analyzing the relationship between monomers and their corresponding polymers through linear regression, we then use integer programming to identify the most accurate molecular formula that fits the data. This technique is demonstrated using a dataset of organic inorganic polymers, resulting in accurate inferences of molecular weights and formulas for various polymers, including those made up of multiple types of monomers.

Detecting tumors in the esophagus using CT scans is crucial for effective treatment planning. However, this process is challenging due to the low contrast between tumors and surrounding tissue, as well as the varying shape and location of the esophagus in different patients. To address these challenges, a new deep learning model called the Esophageal tumor segmentation using a Dilated Dense Focus Unet (DDAUnet) is proposed. This model combines several advanced techniques, including skip connections, residual connections, and knowledge from adjacent anatomical structures to improve segmentation accuracy. The DDAUnet uses dilated and dense blocks to capture both local and global features, while a focus map is generated to highlight the location of the esophagus in each slice of the CT scan. This location information is then used to guide the segmentation process, resulting in more accurate segmentation of the esophagus and any tumors present. The proposed model is evaluated on two public datasets and shows superior performance compared to several state-of-the-art methods.

Multilingualism is a defining characteristic of many communities worldwide.  While it brings opportunities for social and economic growth, it also presents challenges due to language barriers.  These challenges can hinder effective communication and cooperation among individuals who speak different languages.  As a result, there is a pressing need to develop artificial intelligence systems that can effectively process and understand multiple languages simultaneously.  Although research has been conducted on monolingual systems and separate languages, there is limited exploration into the complexities of multilingualism and the unique communication patterns that arise from it.  This paper delves into the intricacies of multilingualism and presents a case for investigating multilingual natural language processing (NLP) using mixed-language text as a starting point.  This type of text, which combines two or more languages in a single utterance, is prevalent in multilingual societies and poses unique challenges for NLP tasks.  While there are significant technical challenges associated with mixed-language text, there are also non-technical factors that can influence the success of such systems, including sociolinguistic and psycholinguistic influences.  This paper outlines these additional factors and their implications for the development of AI systems for multilingual societies.  By considering these diverse influences, researchers can create more effective and inclusive AI systems for multilingual communities.

Human benchmark datasets are commonly used to evaluate the performance of automated image captioning systems. These datasets consist of descriptions provided by humans in response to corresponding images. However, their utility is limited due to several critical issues. Firstly, the lack of information about how these datasets were assembled hinders our understanding of their underlying structure and content. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted an in-depth analysis of three widely recognized benchmark datasets: MS-COCO, VGG, and Flickr30k. Our examination focused on various aspects, including the age and demographics of participants, the language proficiency of contributors, and the linguistic features present in the data. Furthermore, we explored the interplay between these datasets and current image captioning models. Our findings reveal that a significant portion of benchmark datasets may already be partially annotated through existing datasets, and that their limited diversity restricts their effectiveness in assessing the capabilities of state-of-the-art models.

Researchers have extensively studied Ta$_2$O$_5$, a material with a complex lattice structure, to understand its electronic and optical properties. The lattice structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ is particularly intricate, with multiple nearly equivalent configurations that make it difficult to predict its behavior. To address this challenge, we employed density functional theory to identify 120 unique lattice configurations and used Monte Carlo simulations to determine the most stable configuration. The results of our simulations reveal that the lattice structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ exhibits metallic properties and that the most stable configuration is highly sensitive to temperature and pressure. Furthermore, we found that the lattice structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ undergoes a phase transition at a critical temperature and pressure, with the resulting structure displaying unique electronic and optical properties. The research also reveals that the lattice structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ is intimately linked to its semiconducting behavior and that the material's dielectric properties are strongly influenced by its lattice structure. The results of our research provide valuable insights into the lattice structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ and its semiconducting behavior, with implications for the development of novel electronic and photonic devices.

Our study examines how Reddit users' geographic mobility influences their engagement with fake news, focusing on a large-scale migration event in 2019 that saw over one million Americans relocate. We analyzed more than 1.5 million Reddit comments from 11 popular subreddits, correlating the language of users with their speech patterns in their original and new states. Our findings reveal that users who relocated to a different state showed a higher likelihood of interacting with fake news content in their new state's subreddits, particularly when the new state had a lower socioeconomic status than their original state. Additionally, we discovered that the migration event led to a significant increase in fake news circulation in the states where users had relocated to, especially when they came from areas with a higher socioeconomic status. Our research highlights the importance of considering geographic mobility in understanding the spread of fake news and provides valuable insights for designing interventions to limit its impact.

Humans can communicate complex instructions to robots through natural language, a skill that becomes especially valuable when dealing with novel tasks.  To better understand the types of information conveyed in verbal demonstrations, we conducted an analysis of audio recordings from a dataset consisting of 85 tasks performed by a skilled demonstrator.  Our investigation revealed that the audio signals contain a rich structure that can be effectively used to predict the content of accompanying task descriptions.  A key aspect of this structure is a set of acoustic features that can be linked to specific categories of information contained in the task descriptions.  Our findings provide valuable insights for future research in both automatic instruction learning and teaching-effectiveness optimization.

The intricate behavior of irrational second-level polynomial conformal field theories is investigated through the lens of the dynamical Euler-Arnold equations, revealing a direct correspondence between the theory's irrationality and the chaotic behavior of the equations. This research reveals that the correlation functions in irrational second-level polynomial CFTs exhibit stochastic properties akin to random walks, and the Liouville one-point function in the natural vacuum state reveals a self-similar pattern.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous in our daily lives, and as a result, the importance of ensuring their reliability and correctness is escalating. To address this need, we have developed a novel automated testing framework specifically tailored for conversational systems. This framework enables the creation of tests that simulate real user interactions with applications, thereby ensuring their correctness and robustness. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this system, we employed it to identify bugs in two well-known applications, specifically Slack and Facebook Messenger. Furthermore, we have made this automated testing framework publicly available on GitHub for community use and contribution.

Recommendation systems face a significant challenge known as data sparsity, which hampers their effectiveness. While collaborative filtering has been widely used to address this issue, existing methods often rely on simple graph-based models that fail to fully capture the intricate relationships in user-item interactions. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that simultaneously trains on multiple sparse domains to improve recommendation performance. To achieve this, MSDCR incorporates an innovative data augmentation technique called Domain Adversarial Training (DAT) to capture a comprehensive understanding of user preferences across various aspects. Furthermore, MSDCR incorporates a novel preference enhancement module called Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (CAPL) to better model the complex relationships in user-item interactions. Our experimental results on three real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of MSDCR compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Convex optimization is a rapidly growing field, and optimization methods based on interior cones play a crucial role in various applications, including optimization theory, control systems, and operations research. However, studying these methods, particularly natural gradient descent and Newton's method, in conic spaces is a challenging task due to the inherent complexity of the mathematics involved. In this paper, we develop a general framework for natural conic equations that allows for a straightforward implementation, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to second-order conic problems using the Julia package Hypatia.jl. Our research reveals that, for natural Newton methods, choosing a specific interior point solver is unnecessary, and we provide numerical results to support these findings.

The rapid advancement of MRI technology has significantly improved medical imaging, leading to a surge in automated analysis techniques. However, the efficacy of these analyses heavily relies on the quality assurance of MRI scans, a time-consuming and specialized process. In this study, we propose a deep learning-based method to automatically assess the quality of MRI scans, overcoming the limitations of manual quality control. Our method trains a neural network to classify scan quality using reference images and achieves high accuracy, as demonstrated in the paper with an average F1-score of 0.85 on the ADNI dataset. The results indicate that our approach can effectively evaluate the quality of MRI scans and may have significant implications for the widespread adoption of automated analysis techniques.

This study focuses on how private electric vehicles influence the resilience of power distribution networks during extreme weather events. By defining resilience as the ability to restore critical services after a disturbance, we incorporate PEV charging behavior into our analysis. Using a case study in New York City, we model PEV charging decisions during weather emergencies through a multi-agent optimization framework. We represent the recovery process as a two-stage optimization problem, accounting for the repair of damaged grid components and the restoration of outaged areas. By integrating PEV charging into our analysis, we evaluate the vulnerability of the grid to weather-related disruptions. We develop a metric to quantify this risk and apply it to our case study, revealing that weather emergencies can lead to significant PEV service interruptions. Furthermore, we investigate the role of PEVs in delaying the restoration process and identify key factors that exacerbate this issue.

The concept of complex social interactions, such as multi-agent meetings, is a fascinating aspect of our reality. In this work, we explore the intricacies of these interactions by employing a novel design framework that utilizes drive-based motivation to accomplish a recurring meeting between two agents. To do this, we utilize a recurrent policy that allows each agent to make decisions independently, guided by their individual desires to reach the meeting. Our results demonstrate that this approach enables agents to successfully plan and execute recurring meetings in a consistent and reliable manner.

This research focuses on examining the structural, electronic and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3 and the solid solution Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn3. Using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the density functional theory framework, we investigated the structural stability of these materials in different crystallographic structures. Our results indicate that GdSn3 and CmSn3 exhibit a complex antiferromagnetic ground state within the Sc3In3 structure. Additionally, we found that GdSn3 displays a half-metallic behavior, whereas CmSn3 shows a ferrimagnetic metallic state. The magnetic moment of GdSn3 is 7.0 $\mu_B$, while CmSn3 has a magnetic moment of 0.6 $\mu_B$. The magnetic moment of GdSn3 remains unchanged in the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn3 series, whereas CmSn3 shows a significant increase in magnetic moment with a higher Gd concentration. The calculated magnetic susceptibility of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn3 is 0.00011 emu.

A table is compiled that projects the number of baryons and mesons expected in various celestial bodies, including stars, planets, moons, asteroids, comets, and interstellar gas clouds.  The mass of each object is converted to the number of protons, and the results are expressed in units of $10^{57}$ protons.  The data for solid objects is drawn from established sources, whereas the interstellar objects have estimates based on their mass densities.  The table is organized into categories for stars, planets, moons, small solar system bodies, and interstellar objects.

A key component in Euclidean geometry is the Fano theorem, which has a proof that relies on the properties of vectors. In a non-Archimedean setting, the Fano theorem's proof can be derived using vector space principles. However, the Coxeter group $K$ has a more complex geometric structure than a vector space, making it unclear whether the foundation theorem for B-type groups, proven by Tignol and Amour, can be simplified using the same approach. In this study, we establish a "generalized foundation theorem" that encompasses the Tignol-Amour theorem and the fano theorem, both of which can be seen as specific instances. By doing so, we develop a more straightforward proof for the Tignol-Amour theorem.

A new method for cosmological parameter estimation has been developed, utilizing weak lensing effects on Type Ia supernovae to extract information from large-scale structure. Our approach leverages the fact that the magnification bias in supernova observations provides insights into the distribution of matter, enabling us to estimate the matter density and the product of the matter and dark energy densities' fluctuations. By incorporating these estimates into a likelihood function and combining it with Planck CMB data, we can constrain cosmological parameters. Applying this method to the Pantheon sample of supernovae and estimating the impact of intrinsic scatter and selection bias on the data, we found that our analysis yields results comparable to traditional lensing-independent analyses. Moreover, our analysis is sensitive to weak lensing effects, allowing us to estimate the influence of the supernovae's progenitors on the distribution of matter around them. Our results indicate that the intrinsic scatter and selection bias have a minimal effect on our analysis, and that our approach can be used to study the relationship between the formation of galaxies and the formation of matter and dark energy structures on large scales.

T-shaped waveguides are fundamental components in photonic integrated circuits, and their performance is heavily influenced by their material properties. We investigated the characteristics of T-shaped silicon waveguides operating in the telecommunication wavelength range, revealing that their transmission behavior is not linearly proportional to their arm widths. A non-monotonic transmission pattern was observed, with a distinct inflection point at 0.5 µm, which coincides with the transition from silicon substrate leakage to radiation into the superstrate. This discovery is significant as it marks the boundary between two distinct regimes of T node behavior.

Context-aware detection is a significant advancement in the field of object detection, enabling systems to not only identify objects but also comprehend their relationships within a scene. While current research primarily focuses on enhancing detection accuracy, a notable gap exists in evaluating the influence of complex scene contexts on the performance of object detectors. In this work, we investigate the impact of context on detector performance by employing context-aware segmentation masks to refine training data. The results obtained using this approach are then compared to those achieved with traditional pixel-level annotations. The experiment reveals that context is a challenging aspect for detectors to process, and we further explore the underlying reasons behind this difficulty.

This study focuses on a specific nonhomogeneous Kirchhoff type elliptic system that is set within a two-dimensional bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^2$. The system is characterized by the competition between the Trudinger-Moser functionals of two kinds of exponential growth rates and the elliptic operator. Through careful analysis, we establish the existence of a nontrivial solution to this system, taking into consideration the Kirchhoff effects and the competitive interactions at play.

We derive a series of sub-Gaussian tail bounds for the squared sum of binary random variables that exhibit diverse forms of negative correlation, encompassing both pairwise and stronger forms of correlation. These results provide an improved range of bounds compared to existing literature, particularly for randomly permuted data. Our approach utilizes the method of bounded ratios to derive our sub-Gaussian tail bounds. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical application of our findings in the context of statistical hypothesis testing, specifically for testing the null distribution of linear regression coefficients.

A key question in the study of symplectic geometry is whether two compatible complex structures that yield the same underlying symplectic structure can be transformed into each other through a specific type of transformation known as a symplectic diffeomorphism. In this paper, we investigate this question within the context of compact symplectic manifolds and identify specific conditions under which the answer is positive. In particular, we demonstrate that the answer is yes when the compatible complex structures correspond to certain types of integrable almost complex structures, provided the underlying symplectic manifold has a sufficiently small first Betti number.

Incompatible kidney transplants can be significantly improved by accepting kidneys that don't match well, a process influenced by various factors. We've developed a mathematical model to determine the most effective way to accept these kidneys, considering how they affect waiting list candidates and how quickly the donated kidney lasts. Our analysis reveals that the optimal level of acceptance varies depending on the quality of the donated kidney, and we've found that ignoring the "death-censored waiting time" can lead to less effective outcomes. Ultimately, our study provides insights into how to best utilize these donated kidneys to improve the chances of a successful transplant for patients waiting for a match.

This paper conducts a comprehensive analysis of the Loughran-McDonald financial word polarity dataset, which contains over 55,000 words annotated for their emotional content, by employing natural language understanding techniques. Our primary objective is to determine if the famous NLP task of semantic similarity can be applied to this dataset. Our findings reveal significant discrepancies between the semantic relationships derived from word embeddings and human intuition, particularly when using a simple cosine similarity metric. Our results indicate that the embeddings do not accurately capture the emotional content of the dataset, as evidenced by the low correlation between human-rated semantic similarity and cosine similarity. Our paper presents a detailed discussion on the implications of these findings for financial NLP and presents a set of experiments to further investigate the emotional content of the dataset.

This article provides the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based Integrated Data and Energy Delivery (IODE) frameworks for counteracting energy decay in wireless power transfer systems over long transmission distances. We derive and analyze the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM IODE optimizers, revealing that the SISO-OFDM IODE can be viewed as a component of the MISO-OFDM IODE. A numerical example is presented to illustrate the benefits of employing multiple transmitters and OFDM in IODE systems.

A significant issue with deep reinforcement learning in multiplayer games is its lack of transparency in decision-making. In order to address this problem, we are developing a framework that integrates the best available explanation methods with reinforcement learning, resulting in a novel approach called FEAR (Multiplayer Reinforcement Learning That Produces Best Response Equilibrium Explanations). This approach enables a player to make informed decisions that align with rational behavior, based on a compact and interpretable representation of the game. We have applied this framework to a complex variant of the starcraft, known as the brood warfare, in a three-player version, and have developed a set of explicit explanations for rational behavior that can be used to generate actions for rational opponents in the game.

We're examining how an epidemic spreads through a network of nodes that can form new connections, specifically in a setting where the network structure is static. We're focusing on a type of connection formation model, known as the random triadic formation model, and simulating the spread of an SIR epidemic using the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered framework. Our study reveals that as the intensity of incoming connections increases, the number of nodes that recover and leave the network also rises, leading to a sudden and sharp outbreak in moderate to high connectivity environments. We've discovered that the connections formed between nodes, rather than those they prevent, are primarily responsible for this phenomenon. We've also found that the environment in which these connections form, whether it's competitive or cooperative, doesn't significantly impact the overall results.

This paper presents a structured approach to creating a statistical model for particle physics, focusing on the specific task of determining the parton distribution functions (PDFs) in hadrons. We begin by outlining the fundamental equations and concepts, and then outline the specific calculations required to make a numerical model that can be compared to experimental data. This involves breaking down the various components of the measured cross sections into their contributing parts, each with its own PDF dependence. As the order of calculations increases in QCD, the number of relevant processes to consider grows, and we also need to account for the effects of higher twists and other corrections. The framework we describe is designed to be easily adaptable to the specific needs of PDF fitting programs, and we illustrate its application by considering the determination of the strange quark distribution in the proton.

To further optimize reinforcement learning algorithms' sample efficiency and accelerate their convergence, existing methods have limited success by incorporating randomness in value function updates through experience replay. In contrast, this study investigates alternative ways to reduce the impact of subsequent iterations' cumulative reward errors, exploring the effectiveness of reducing the variance of the policy's state visitation distribution. Our proposed strategy, known as variance diminution based experience replay (V-DiER), dynamically prioritizes replaying less visited states by allocating more replay samples to states with higher uncertainty. We demonstrate the benefits of V-DiER through successful integration into multiple off-policy algorithms, including DQN, PPO, and SAC, achieving improved performance in various control tasks and complex multi-agent environments.

In our study, we developed MultiTalk, a complex conversation dataset comprising 119 highly interconnected dialogue threads, where each participant experienced at least three distinct conversational directions. We examined the characteristics of our single-session and our unique all-session combined dataset, providing a comprehensive reference for future research.

We present a novel implementation of f(R) gravity within the GADGET-4 code, enabling the simulation of modified gravity scenarios at the same speed as general relativity. Our method involves mapping modified gravity models to their equivalent D6 RHD counterparts, allowing us to utilize existing simulations to compare and contrast the two theories. We developed a customized library of modified gravity initial conditions and verification tests to ensure the accuracy of our code, passing all tests successfully. We then used our code to produce high-resolution modified gravity simulations, finding that they matched lower-resolution GR simulations in terms of matter power spectrum and halo mass function. We also found that our code's modified gravity simulations could be made indistinguishable from GR simulations by adjusting a key parameter, further demonstrating the efficiency and effectiveness of our implementation. Our results show that efficient, accurate modified gravity simulations are now possible, providing researchers with a valuable tool for investigating the nature of gravity on cosmological scales.
