In this paper, we delve into the practical challenges of deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices and introduce the concept of Spiking Random Neural Networks (SPARNN) as a potential solution. We explain how the application of random projections in the early stages of a neural network can streamline data processing with minimal computational cost, enabling real-time classification using efficient spike-based operations. By combining the benefits of compressing the data dimensionality and leveraging the energy-saving properties of SPNNs, we demonstrate the versatility of the SPARNN framework through various implementations, including a fully customizable SPARNN and a streamlined version that leverages an existing ANN. Through comprehensive experiments, we validate the effectiveness of the framework in achieving precise and low-energy real-time classification tasks.

The equilibrium quark distribution is re-evaluated within a thermal bath, taking into account the influence of a strong magnetic field and the polarization of spins. The resulting calculation of the integral over the transverse momentum reveals that the strength of the interaction between polarized and unpolarized strange stars significantly varies depending on the presence of the magnetic field. The thermal equation of state is derived and its characteristics are examined in the context of the polarization of a star composed of strange quarks. The equation of state is then utilized to investigate the behavior of polarized strange quark matter under conditions of thermal equilibrium and infinite density. The conditions required for the formation of polarized strange quark stellar remnants are also determined.

In 1983, Fournier introduced the concept of a $\{2,4\}$-factorization for cubic graphs with at most 4 imperfect matchings. This paper proves a stronger statement, demonstrating that such graphs can be decomposed into two ideal 2-factors. Specifically, we show that if a cubic graph G has a not-possible-3-edge-colourable structure and possesses a perfect 2-factorization, then G can be broken down into two ideal 2-factors.

This paper introduces the concept of "timeloops," an adaptive reinforcement learning approach designed to optimize system call policies for a Containerized HTTP Server, Apache2. By integrating the removal of the no-call strategy and the use of a linear function approximator, it enhances the efficiency of training and the quality of learned policies. The application of this method to a real-world scenario is demonstrated through the optimization of HTTP server call policies in a containerized environment, with successful results achieved in a simulated microservice architecture. The source code for the project is made available on GitHub at https://github.com/chenyutw/timeloops.

This study introduces a new filtering method for a specific type of probability process model that's defined over continuous physical space. It achieves this by developing an updated Particle Mean Birth Resampling (PMBMR) algorithm tailored for managing sensor resources. The approach involves creating potential particle positions on a discrete grid and adjusting the number of particles in response to information from available sensors. The effectiveness of this new filter is demonstrated through numerical simulations for tracking multiple moving targets using real sensors.

This study examines the null controllability of a biological population model that includes an interior decay term. The population is represented by a function satisfying the Helmholtz equation in a given domain, and evolves over time. The decay term, which is located in a specific sub-region, is designed to be non-zero only within that area. The research demonstrates the existence of a control function, applied to a specific part of the domain during a given time period, capable of driving the population to zero in a smaller, possibly smaller, sub-region. The proof relies on a combination of mathematical techniques, including duality arguments, observability inequalities, and Carleman estimates, which are designed to handle non-convex domains.

Strengthening the capabilities of soccer robots in high-pressure situations, such as free kicks and penalty kicks, is a pressing challenge in soccer robot competitions. Penalty kicks are particularly crucial, as they can significantly influence the outcome of a match. To excel in these scenarios, the robots must make lightning-fast decisions within a mere 100 milliseconds, determining the optimal approach to the ball while analyzing the goalkeeper's position. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel, modular action selection system that leverages a reinforcement learning-based method to evaluate actions in real-time. This system has been successfully applied to the SoccerRobots world championship, and our approach has been shown to outperform previous methods in recent competitions.

Recently, there has been a significant interest in expanding research into source inversion within seismology. Although initial findings are promising, it is crucial to account for larger and more complex sources, such as fault slips, in order to fully understand the signals recorded at individual seismic stations. Current methods typically utilize point-source models, ignoring the sources' finite size. In this study, we explore the potential of simultaneously recovering both source parameters and waveforms from recorded data. By developing a comprehensive likelihood function and an efficient gradient calculation method, we can efficiently calculate likelihoods and gradients in a time-domain simulation framework. When testing our method on synthetic data, we found that it can accurately recover source parameters and even small details of the source structure. We also demonstrate the feasibility of including the energy partition of shear, compressional, and surface waves in the likelihood function. However, as the computational cost of our method is relatively high, future advancements in reducing computational expenses will be necessary to apply this approach to real recorded data.

A dynamic model is proposed to depict the interplay between species competition and dispersal, accounting for environmental noise. The model combines a noisy nonlocal competition term with a stochastic diffusion term. Analyzing the model's deterministic version reveals a competition-colonization scenario where the noise's impact is then examined. The study shows that high noise levels lead to the elimination of the smaller species, while moderate levels result in coexistence. The model's outcomes are further illustrated through simulations of species population densities.

A novel integrated data and energy networking cognitive D2D model is proposed, which incorporates external surface aids. In this proposed model, cognitive D2D links are based on an market-driven principle, allowing them to access licensed spectrum without causing interference to primary communications. A key aspect of this model involves cognitive users employing an external surface to boost signal transmission to primary communications without causing any disruption. After formulating key performance indicators, including communication efficiency, energy effectiveness, and fairness, we develop a cognitive market game to find the optimal balance between these indicators. Numerical results are then used to evaluate the model's performance.

This study investigates the capabilities of single-point laser Doppler velocimetry (LDV) systems in obtaining two-dimensional velocity measurements remotely. Our research expands upon previous studies that demonstrated the calibration of such systems. By using a rotating disc, we obtained a calibration that is highly accurate, with an uncertainty of less than 0.1%. Furthermore, we successfully obtained a calibration of the LDV system's sensitivity to the direction of motion, which is essential for measuring the direction of motion without additional sensors. With this calibration, we were able to obtain a 2D measurement of the velocity of a rotating disc remotely, with an uncertainty of less than 0.2%. This study provides a detailed account of the calibration and data analysis methods used, as well as the limitations of the system.

In transmission electron microscopy, correctors are used to counteract phase distortions that hinder high-resolution imaging. Currently, correctable distortions are limited to low orders due to the hardware used. This research proposes a new solution: a phase correctable plate made of liquid crystal, capable of handling high-order distortions, including those affecting sub-angstrom resolution. By utilizing a 3D printing master mold and a liquid crystal injection system, a prototype device was created and tested. The results demonstrate that this new correctable plate can achieve high-resolution imaging, surpassing 1 Angstrom. Furthermore, the research highlights the benefits of this new solution, including its flexibility and real-time adjustability, and discusses potential future advancements.

We provide a comprehensive examination of the spectral and orbital stability for the following equation:
$$
  \partial_t^2 u - \Delta u + \left(1-u^2\right)^s = 0
$$
where $u$ is a function of time and space variables, and $s$ is a parameter that can be either greater than zero or equal to one half. This equation arises from its stationary solutions, which are defined by the harmonic map heat flow. We find that the spectral and orbital properties of the ground state remain unchanged under various conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate the orbital stability for certain excited states when the equation is one-dimensional.

We derive several new results concerning rational star-skew matrices over a specific type of non-commutative number field that lacks commutativity, denoted as A. These results mirror the classical theorems of Kronecker and Leopoldt found in standard number theory. In particular, we establish the fact that a matrix $T$ over $A$ has a higher rank than expected, given that it has a reduced rank of 3, this increased rank allows for a representation of $T$ as a part of a matrix constructed from elements within the non-commutative field A.

In the context of Belle II, we investigate the potential of the ALPS II experiment to identify axion-like particles (ALPs) that were previously undetectable through standard model interactions, specifically from $B$ meson decays. We determine the ALPS II detection efficiency for ALPs produced in $B$ meson decays at KEKB, and find that the combined data from both $B$ meson decay modes could enable the ALPS II collaboration to set stringent limits on ALP interactions, surpassing current constraints from standard collider and fixed-target experiments.

We conducted an in-depth analysis of existing approaches to detect semantic inconsistencies between statements and supporting passages, building on our previously introduced task of semantic alteration. Our examination focused specifically on existing contextualized language models, revealing both successful applications and limitations. We found that architectures based on bi-directional embeddings achieved high performance in document retrieval scenarios but struggled with shorter text pairs. Conversely, models designed for question-answering demonstrated greater robustness against manipulated passages, particularly when utilizing contextual features for classification. Notably, models incorporating bi-directional classification exhibited superior performance compared to those using only unidirectional embeddings for classification purposes. Our analysis also highlighted the importance of careful preprocessing and parameter selection in achieving optimal results. To address the lack of standardized evaluation protocols, we developed a unified dataset and benchmark, enabling fair comparisons across different models. Our findings provide valuable insights for future research and practical applications in the field of natural language processing.

The spin properties of heavy quasar absorbers can be effectively modeled using the Drude-Pearson approach, which accounts for the random alignment of individual angular momenta. Our analysis of 20 heavy quasar systems reveals that the spin angular momenta are preferentially aligned, contradicting the expected random distribution. This deviation from a uniform distribution is quantified by an alignment factor, which is found to be significantly greater than one. This unexpected result may be attributed to the formation of massive compact objects through the collapse of a gas disk, which is a plausible mechanism for superradiance-induced particle mass formation. Based on this hypothesis, we derive an upper limit for the mass of ultralight scalar, pseudoscalar, or vector bosons, which is estimated to be less than 10^-19 times the mass of a proton for ultralight bosons.

A phenomenon called interkinetic nuclear movement (INM) is observed in developing neural tissues, where nuclei migrate between the apical surface and the base of a tissue in sync with the cell cycle. Although INM was first described in the mid-20th century, its underlying cause is still not fully understood. A hypothesis suggests that INM is driven by the movement of neuroblasts through the tissue, but this is contradicted by evidence showing that INM continues even when cell division is prevented. To investigate INM further, we utilized a particle-tracking method on live zebrafish retina, which allowed us to analyze the motion of nuclei in retinas where the cells had divided and those that hadn't. Our findings revealed that INM behaves like a diffusive process, with nuclei moving back and forth across the retinal surface. We also discovered that the speed of INM is influenced by the temperature of the environment, and that the cells undergoing INM are significantly larger than those that have divided. These results suggest that INM may be a byproduct of the physical properties of cells, rather than a mechanism to move through the tissue.

In this work, we investigate a specific application of source separation coding, which involves reconstructing multiple related videos from compressed and noisy data obtained from a single video camera. We propose a novel approach that leverages a two-channel encoder to facilitate reconstruction by a variational autoencoder, which utilizes temporal consistency as a prior for reconstruction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through extensive experiments on reconstructing multiple videos from a single camera's data, showing that our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art in various metrics.

A comprehensive computer simulation has been carried out to examine the effects of dimensionality on the critical behavior of incompressible polar active fluids under conditions of dimensional quenched disorder, across various spatial dimensions from 3 to 5 dimensions. The simulations involved solving the dynamic equations of motion for $10^6$ active particles, each undergoing stochastic collisions. The upper critical dimension has been confirmed to be 4, with distinct critical exponents observed for dimensions both above and below this critical point. The scaling and collapse of order parameters have been demonstrated, along with the effects of disorder on the dynamics of these active fluids.

In recent years, the amount of paperwork has surged, prompting the need for a more efficient data collection process. One method to achieve this is through the use of optical character recognition (OCR) and natural language processing (NLP) to extract information from Indonesian identity cards. This research focuses on developing an automated system to capture and interpret the text within these documents. The system employs Tesseract 4 for OCR and a Conditional Random Field (CRF) algorithm for NLP, with the goal of creating a user-friendly tool for data entry. The proposed system's performance was evaluated using mean average precision (MAP) and F-score metrics, yielding results of 0.94 and 0.94, respectively.

We present a novel approach to solving the quantum harmonic oscillator in the presence of a time-varying force, employing the path integral formulation. By utilizing the properties of Gaussian integrals and applying Metropolis-Hastings and Hybrid Monte Carlo algorithms, we calculate the propagator for this system. Our method yields the same results as traditional solutions, and our approach can be easily adapted to solve more complex problems.

The YORP effect's impact on a rotating asteroid is characterized by the acceleration it produces. To determine the YORP acceleration, the rotational period and axis of rotation of the asteroid are required. We have calculated the YORP acceleration for the asteroids 1992 SK, Toro, and Geographos using shape models and light curve data. The calculated YORP acceleration values are as follows: YORP19=0.0004±0.0001 rad/s^2 for 1992 SK, 0.0014±0.0004 rad/s^2 for Toro, and 0.0004±0.0001 rad/s^2 for Geographos. The estimated ranges of YORP acceleration for these asteroids are as follows: 0.0003-0.0006 rad/s^2 for 1992 SK, 0.0008-0.0020 rad/s^2 for Toro, and 0.0002-0.0006 rad/s^2 for Geographos.

We establish the non-joiness of collections of homeomorphisms of a surface, denoted as $\Homeo_0(\Sigma)$, when equipped with the topology of uniform convergence on compacta. This outcome is achieved by proving the non-joiness of the subset of volume-preserving homeomorphisms, represented as $\Diff_1(\Sigma)$. These proofs are accomplished by demonstrating the non-joiness of the subsets of homeomorphisms that shift the measure of specific test sets in the plane, in upward or downward directions, symbolized as $\Shift_+(\R^2,\mu)$ and $\Shift_-(\R^2,\mu)$, respectively. The non-joiness of these particular subsets is further illustrated through explicit examples.

We establish a computable extension of the theory of infinite words that is of type $ \omega $ in the effective regular fragment, demonstrating that it precisely corresponds to Wilkie's well-known description of the same part of logic.

A key feature of complex systems is multistability, where multiple stable states can exist simultaneously. A common way to analyze these systems is through basins of attraction, which map out the regions leading to each state. A notable aspect of these regions is fractal boundaries, which exhibit self-similar patterns at various scales. A new method has been developed to study the intricate geometry of these boundaries using a combination of techniques, including the correlation dimension and wavelet-based entropy measures. This approach reveals that the boundaries often display disordered yet repeating patterns, which can be visualized through the creation of self-similar maps. A case study of the Lorenz system with specific parameters (sigma=10, omega=0.25, and beta=8/3) demonstrates the method's effectiveness in revealing the complex structure of its two coexisting attractors.

We establish a second-order convergence method for calculating the reachable sets in control systems subject to constraints. Our approach involves applying a range-width formula to a variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, resulting in a computational algorithm that achieves second-order accuracy. This is in contrast to existing methods, which typically only achieve first-order accuracy when using similar algorithms.

The ventral temporal cortex, a brain region responsible for processing the meaning of words, contains an area that specifically responds to animate entities such as people and animals. The underlying reason for this distinct animacy-based sensitivity remains unclear. A leading theory suggests that this sensitivity is a fundamental property of the anatomy of this brain region. In contrast, a competing hypothesis proposes that it is a result of the language we use, which frequently categorizes entities based on their animacy. To differentiate between these two possibilities, we conducted computational modeling using 1000 neural networks that were trained to recognize patterns in images. Our models demonstrated that the networks that were trained to replicate the activity of the brain's visual processing areas would not have a specific animacy-based region, whereas those that were trained natural language to understand the meaning of words would. This finding supports the idea that the animacy-based area is a product of the language we use, rather than a fundamental property of the anatomy of this brain region.

We demonstrate the quantum unique ergodicity of the first quantum chaos conjecture with enhanced efficiency, specifically for the associated measures of the $L^2$-normalized Hecke-Maass newforms in the full spectral parameter range. Additionally, we derive the absence of the Landau-Siegel zeros.

We have developed quantum relational Hoare reasoning framework that incorporates "expectations" into the reasoning process, which is a generalization of invariants used in both single-program and inter-process verification. This framework allows for proving correctness of a wide range of algorithms, including those with dynamic memory allocation, by defining pre- and postconditions as functions that take two programs and output a relational predicate. These conditions specify when equivalent programs produce equivalent outputs.

The rapid transmission of infectious diseases is significantly influenced by the presence of super-spreader events, where a single individual unknowingly transmits the pathogen to a large number of people. To investigate the effects of these occurrences, we developed an SIR model that simulates the transmission dynamics of a pandemic. Our research reveals that super-spreader events can lead to a rapid decline in susceptible populations, particularly when transmission rates are high. The location of these events plays a crucial role in determining the overall impact, with events occurring in areas with high concentrations of susceptible individuals resulting in the most severe outcomes. The timing of these events is also significant, with events occurring early in the pandemic leading to more severe consequences than those occurring later. Furthermore, we found that the spatial distribution of the population plays a key role in determining the effects of these occurrences. Our research has implications for public health policy, emphasizing the importance of early and widespread interventions to prevent the rapid transmission of infectious diseases.

A collection of linear operators acting on a complex topological vector space is termed cyclic if there exists a vector that, when subjected to the operators in the collection, generates a dense subset within the vector space. This research paper explores the properties and applications of cyclic sets of operators, building upon the concept of cyclic operators individually examined in previous studies. It proves the stability of cyclic sets of operators under the addition of single cyclic operators and under taking powers of polynomial transformations of the集合. Additionally, it provides a characterization of the ideal of non-cosingular operators within the ring of operator polynomials.

The study focuses on addressing and mitigating bias in inferred measurements of solar vector magnetic fields, which are commonly obtained through a technique known as Stokes inversion. Researchers have developed a new method, the Inversion Bias Estimator (IBE), to assess this type of systematic error. The IBE method involves creating artificial polarimetric spectra based on actual observations, subjecting them to various inversion and line selection processes, and then comparing the results to the initial parameters. The IBE approach was applied to four prominent inversion codes using spectral data from the Fe I 6302 Angstrom line, revealing significant variations in the inferred field values among the codes. The study demonstrates that the IBE method can be employed to adjust inversion results, thereby reducing discrepancies among different codes. Furthermore, the IBE method is shown to be effective in assessing inversion accuracy when ground-based spectral data are used.

A sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations severely hampers the modeling of certain quantum systems with intricate fermionic correlations and in a variety of scenarios featuring a complex Fermi surface. A persistent and exponentially growing negative probability in path integral simulations leads to an intractable issue. We propose a novel variational approach utilizing a complex-valued neural network to approximate the wave function within a Markov Chain Monte Carlo framework, bypassing the sign problem. Our method successfully overcomes the sign problem in a one-dimensional Hubbard model at half-filling and maintains accuracy in a parameter range that traditional variational Monte Carlo techniques struggle with.

Given a free monoid defined by a set of free generators and a recognition automaton with finite states, we define topological entropy and topological complexity as measures of a language's combinatorial and structural dynamics. For two languages within the free monoid, the conditions under which the product of these languages has a non-zero measure and the complexity and entropy of the resulting language are directly related to those of the original languages when a homomorphism is applied are examined. Additionally, the conditions under which the complement of the product of these languages has a non-zero measure and the complexity and entropy of the resulting language are directly related to those of the original languages are examined. Furthermore, the behavior of topological complexity and entropy of languages is examined in relation to free group languages and the changes in free group basis.

In natural language processing, transfer learning allows models to apply knowledge gained from one task to another, thereby improving efficiency. Although models can transfer learning within the same domain, they struggle when it comes to completely unrelated tasks. Our research focuses on developing a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based method that enables models to generalize across tasks with no related knowledge, even when the target task is completely unrelated to the source task. Our proposed framework consists of two main components: first, we create a vector index from training data to facilitate efficient knowledge retrieval, and second, we leverage this index to enhance a pre-trained model's performance on the target task. Our results from experiments on six different datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method over baseline models, with our proposed retrieval-enhanced model outperforming the best baseline by a significant margin of 4.1 points. Our findings also reveal that the model's performance is heavily influenced by the quality of the vector index, highlighting the importance of efficient knowledge retrieval in cross-task generalization.

Optimizing machine learning models through differential privacy involves selecting a privacy budget, training a model without privacy protection, and then applying privacy to the hyperparameter optimization process of the initial model. Our research proposes a new approach called OPTRV, which combines the flexibility of a privacy-aware optimization method with the efficiency of a retraining strategy. Unlike previous approaches, our method allows for the use of highly effective optimization algorithms in a way that respects the limits of privacy. Our results from multiple deep learning tasks, including classification, ranking, and recommendation, show that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of model performance.

This note explores the lattice of sub-distributions for a specific complex structure previously introduced, which has a similar nature to the Bruhat order within the symmetric group. We identify conditions under which the complex structure of the involutions within the symmetric group forms a distributive structure, and we also determine the modular properties of the complex structure.

To better understand the evolution of the Milky Way galaxy, astronomers analyze the chemical composition of stars within it. We have developed an advanced statistical model using a genetic algorithm to accurately predict star spectra, specifically for a large dataset of over 17,000 stars from APOGEE-1/2. This model determined the chemical makeup of these stars, focusing on 11 key elements, and covered a wide range of physical characteristics. By analyzing these characteristics, we created probability distributions that describe the physical and chemical properties of the galactic disk. We found evidence of at least two distinct populations within the disk, each with unique patterns of chemical composition. Furthermore, we defined new parameters to describe the deviations of a star's chemistry from these populations and used them to investigate the relationships between various physical characteristics and chemical deviations. This study provides a detailed understanding of the diversity of stars within the galactic disk.

A type of social network graph called a spreading process was used to analyze a WeChat post about COVID-19 prevention in China. This allowed for the development of a "spread measure" to quantify how much influence an individual had within the network. This measure was then applied to analyze the dynamics of a specific online rumor in China. The study found that the average influence in the network was not uniform, and that the spread measure could be used to predict the likelihood of a user sharing the rumor. Furthermore, the spread measure was found to be more effective than other existing models in predicting user behavior, and that the network exhibited a small-world property.

A comprehensive study of a galaxy group's evolution can be achieved by analyzing planetary nebulae within its constituent galaxies. Determining the precise distances to these galaxies is a critical step in this analysis. By employing a novel method that utilizes the velocity dispersion of stellar remnants known as white dwarfs, researchers have established an independent distance measurement to the Fornax galaxy cluster. In order to apply this method to the galaxies within the cluster, a catalog of planetary nebulae was created by combining existing data from the literature. This catalog, which contains over 115,000 objects, has been updated and corrected to ensure uniformity in the measurement of radial velocities. By analyzing this catalog for the galaxies IC 1670, NGC 247, and NGC 3628, radial velocity distributions were derived from which distance measurements were obtained using the acceleration due to gravity within the cluster. The resulting estimates for these galaxies are consistent with previously established results within the margin of error. This method, however, is limited by the availability of available data and may not be applicable to all galaxies within the group.

Periodic data streams, commonly used in applications like monitoring, forecasting, and scientific research, require efficient processing engines to handle performance and data management challenges. Existing processing engines, designed for general-purpose stream analytics, struggle to meet the specific needs of periodic data processing. To address this limitation, we present the LifeStream prototype, a specialized processing engine that leverages in-memory data structures and CPU caching mechanisms to optimize periodic data processing performance. The LifeStream prototype incorporates a caching-aware join algorithm and a prefetching mechanism to minimize cache misses and disk I/O operations. Experimental results demonstrate the LifeStream prototype's superior performance compared to conventional processing engines, achieving up to 10x faster query execution and a 50x higher throughput for typical periodic data processing workloads.

This study focuses on establishing the existence of timelike Bertrand curves within a specific type of geometric space, a particular spacetime. It's also worth noting that in a more general context, the necessary and sufficient conditions for the absolute proper curvature functions of such curves are not constant, are defined as $\bar{\varkappa} = \left| \frac{\varkappa_1}{C_2 \pm \sqrt{C_2^2 - \left(\frac{\varkappa_1}{\varkappa_2}\right)^2} \pm \frac{\varkappa_1}{\varkappa_2}} \right|$ and $\bar{\varkappa}_2 = \left| \frac{\varkappa_2}{C_2 \pm \sqrt{C_2^2 - \left(\frac{\varkappa_1}{\varkappa_2}\right)^2} \pm \frac{\varkappa_1}{\varkappa_2}} \right|$, where $C_2$ represents a positive constant.

The choice of loss function in deep learning classification models is typically based on convention rather than a clear understanding of its implications. In this research, we investigate the effects of using non-traditional loss functions, specifically the 1/n-th and n-th powers of the original error measures, on model performance. Our experiments, conducted on multiple datasets and neural network configurations, reveal that the models' performance peaks at an intermediate loss function, suggesting that there is an optimal point beyond which increasing the power of the error measures leads to diminishing returns. We also observed that the point at which the best performance is achieved shifts depending on the neural network's depth and width. Furthermore, we found that the performance of the models remains consistent when the loss measures are scaled, indicating that the models are able to adapt to different loss functions effectively.

This research simulates the complex interplay of mechanical and thermal forces that lead to the development of crystalline structures in polymeric materials. 
A numerical model was developed to capture the evolution of these structures, incorporating statistical and mechanical aspects of polymers, along with advanced simulation techniques. 
To manage computational demands, a novel approach was adopted to represent areas of crystalline and amorphous polymers using probabilistic fields, significantly reducing the number of variables needed for computation. 
To handle computational challenges, efficient solvers and parallel computing methods were employed to manage computational grids and equations. 
The results of these simulations revealed the formation of characteristic polymer structures, including thin, alternating layers of crystalline and amorphous regions, with dimensions on a micrometer scale. 
Our findings demonstrate the ability to accurately replicate strain-induced polymer crystallization through advanced computational simulations.

To understand the mechanism behind the phase transition from nematic superconductivity to the normal state as temperature rises, we must examine two competing processes. The first involves the disruption of electron pairs within triplet Cooper couples due to their magnetic susceptibility, known as Pauli paramagnetism in the nematic state. In contrast, the second process entails the scattering of these couples by thermal fluctuations, leading to the creation of Nambu-Goldstone modes. We utilized the nematic triplet model to calculate the self-energy and the polarization vertex, which allowed us to determine the critical temperature for the transition from the superconducting state to the normal state. Our calculations show that the critical temperature is closely related to the energy scale of nematicity.

A key issue in CPM differential detection is that expanding the signal's spectral efficiency requires processing signals with a larger delay differential, which can be computationally demanding. This paper presents a new approach to address this challenge by using two simple first-order differential detectors and adjusting their differential delays to match the desired, higher delay through the combination of their outputs. This method enables a straightforward implementation of a non-coherent differential detector with a high delay, which is crucial for selecting CPM modulation schemes suitable for power-efficient communication devices. We demonstrate the superiority of this new method over existing techniques by comparing their error performance and computational efficiency, using the 2D and 4D differential detectors as examples. We also provide optimized delay differential settings for a wide range of CPM modulations with a fixed pulse shape and provide a performance-computationality trade-off curve to guide the choice of the best non-coherent differential detector for a specific application.

A key aspect of a quantum channel's characterization is its quantum compressibility, which is defined through the best possible expression of the channel as a combination of its components, including one with zero quantum content. In the case of spacetime, we examine the compressibility of the Minkowski vacuum when influenced by a time-varying detector that acts as a thermal reservoir at a specific temperature. We find that the Minkowski vacuum is incompressible under these conditions, as the quantum cost of the channel remains unchanged even when the detector's characteristics are altered. However, we also explore scenarios where the detector is subject to the uncertainty principle and finds that it exhibits finite compressibility, with the quantum cost of side-channels decreasing as the detector's temperature increases. In the limit of high temperatures, the quantum cost of the detector itself becomes negligible, and the primary source of noise shifts to the fields in the Minkowski vacuum.

We present our latest machine intelligence model, ATOMIC, which comprises an extensive set of reasoning pairs, containing 242,530 entries, where each pair consists of a specific scenario and the subsequent action taken in that situation. To achieve this, we examined the limitations of current datasets and proposed improvements, resulting in an ATOMIC structure with four distinct substructures. Furthermore, we discuss various applications of this rich data set and highlight the challenges in developing machine intelligence for understanding causal relationships.

A significant amount of research and development in the field of quantum computing equipment is being directed towards creating practical and effective applications that can take advantage of emerging quantum hardware. Our team has developed a novel portfolio management tool utilizing the quantum hardware of IBM to evaluate the performance of various portfolio optimization techniques. A benchmark method, which adapts the minimum residual algorithm originally proposed by Harrow et al., is established and modified to function efficiently on current quantum hardware. Our results demonstrate the superiority of a modified version of the Lagrange multiplier algorithm over the benchmark when utilizing low-end quantum hardware, with the performance of both techniques being compared in terms of portfolio size, noise levels, and qubit connectivity. Our study also highlights the importance of portfolio management as a practical application for developing quantum hardware.

In order to enhance the performance of speech recognition systems, a new multi-modal training method is introduced. This approach utilizes a jointly trained neural network that encompasses separate components for processing speech and text data, with a critical focus on specific sections of the text in relation to the corresponding audio segments. A bi-directional focus mechanism is employed to capture the essential information within a particular sound segment, which is then combined to form a comprehensive data point. A newly created multi-modal training set is also presented to facilitate this innovative training method. The proposed approach is demonstrated to be effective through a range of experiments, which involve utilizing pre-trained neural networks and conducting joint training on various datasets.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a specific class of mathematical functions called parking functions. By considering functions from a large finite set of integers, we analyze functions that approach an infinite integer-valued limit as their size increases without bound. We focus on the subset of parking functions and determine the asymptotic distribution of first occurrences of zero in these functions, both in their original and reversed forms. Additionally, by applying techniques from a related study, we establish that in these functions, the infinite lower step function appears, and in many cases, we derive explicit formulas for this function.

We experimentally investigate the impact of a transverse magnetic field on the quantum phase interference of dc SQUIDs made from NbN nanowires in the superconducting state. By applying different magnetic field orientations, we aim to distinguish between two mechanisms responsible for the coherent behavior observed: coherent quantum phase slips and the Coulomb blockade effect. Our findings reveal that the quantum phase interference is influenced by the magnetic field in a manner consistent with the Aharonov-Bohm effect, indicating that our nanosized SQUIDs exhibit coherent quantum phase slips that can be modulated by the transverse magnetic field.

In this paper, we introduce a novel prediction method for New View (NV) images based on dual representation of image features. Our approach leverages a graph structure to depict feature relationships and employs a linear regression model to forecast image projections. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed prediction technique over conventional methods.

Inter-level coupling (ILC) is an emerging phenomenon in spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensates, where two low-lying quasi-energy states become coupled, leading to inter-level Rabi oscillations. In a two-dimensional imbalanced spin component condensate with contact interactions, ILC arises due to the presence of two distinct orbital levels, each occupied by a different spin component. The frequency of inter-level Rabi oscillations is influenced by the relative population of the two orbital levels, the interaction strength, and the tunneling amplitude between the orbital levels. Our research demonstrates the first direct observation of this phenomenon experimentally, revealing that tuning the relative population of the two orbital levels allows for precise control over the frequency of oscillations.

This study focuses on the characteristics of the Omega baryon, a particle with three s quarks and -3 units of strangeness. Since its discovery in 1977 at Brookhaven National Laboratory, efforts have been made to identify this particle at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. A key aspect of research involves studying the full phase space of strange quarks, which is crucial for understanding the formation of hadrons made up of light and strange quarks in the early universe. A critical step in this analysis requires accurate knowledge of the Omega baryon's production cross section for both s and s' (or s, s' and s, s', s) charge exchange reactions.

Our research examines the benefits of using a well-mixed model framework to predict disease transmission in urban buses. We tested this framework's utility by developing and comparing well-mixed models with a more accurate simulation-based approach using Agent-Based Modeling (ABM). Our analysis focused on influenza transmission on buses, considering various transmission probabilities, seating arrangements, and ventilation conditions. We found that despite the complexity of ABM, our well-mixed models accurately predicted the spread of the disease, particularly in scenarios with high transmission risk. The models also successfully captured the relationship between transmission risk and the basic reproduction number ($R_0$), as well as the impact of seating arrangements and ventilation on disease spread. The results indicate that the utility of the well-mixed framework is high, especially when paired with simple data collection methods, and that it can effectively guide public health interventions to reduce the transmission of diseases in urban buses.

The spin-orbit proximity effect in a cobalt layer adjacent to a bismuth interface has been investigated, with a focus on how interfacial bonding influences the spin-orbit coupling and the efficiency of the spin Hall effect. By adjusting the cobalt-bismuth layer thickness ratio, researchers were able to manipulate the efficiency of the inverse spin Hall effect, reaching a maximum at a 1.5 nm cobalt layer. Analysis of the interfacial properties revealed that changing the cobalt-bismuth ratio altered the orbital hybridization and the efficiency of the spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential for tuning the inverse spin Hall effect by manipulating the interfacial properties, offering valuable insights for the development of efficient spintronic devices.

A fractional analogue of generalized Mie-type potential is defined, and its properties are examined. The potential is composed of a sum of three distinct parts: a Coulomb-like term, a harmonic oscillator term, and a power-law term. We investigate how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity is related to overfitting prevention. We show that constraining the norm of a neural network's weights is analogous to limiting its Lipschitz constant, and we explore the impact of various norms on preventing overfitting. We also propose a novel approach that combines the benefits of both techniques and provide both theoretical analysis and a neural network-based algorithm to address the issue of finding an optimal combination.

We investigate the production of Y* dileptons in proton-propton collisions at the LHC for various leptoquark types, specifically t1, b1, t2, and b2, which have large masses and third-generation couplings. Calculations were performed at LHC energies of 7, 8, and 13 Teves. The Y* cross-sections were calculated to next-to-leading order in QCD using MadGraph 5, with PYTHIA 6.4 handling parton showers and hadronization. The Y* mass distribution was analyzed for various masses and production cross-sections were compared to Y production at leading order. The results show that Y* production is concentrated at high transverse momentum and low rapidity, with Y*/Y ratios of 10^-3 to 10^-2, depending on the leptoquark type and LHC energy. The Y*/Y ratios are expected to be higher at forward rapidity. The predictions were also tested against ATLAS data from the 8 TeV LHC run, with reasonable agreement found.

In medical imaging, particularly with Positron Emission Tomography (PET), patients receive ionizing radiation that poses health risks. To mitigate this, PET images are often combined with complementary imaging techniques like computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which provide anatomical details. Leveraging this complementary information, conditional generative models can generate low-dose PET images from high-quality MRI scans. However, these models struggle when dealing with new data outside their training set, a common occurrence in clinical settings. To address this challenge, we present a novel Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Learning (UAML) framework, which estimates data likelihood to quantify uncertainty and selectively train only on reliable, in-distribution data. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that UAML maintains high image quality and structural accuracy, while significantly reducing false uncertainty predictions. Quantitative evaluations further reveal that UAML achieves a 10% improvement in PSNR and a 10.5% reduction in MAE compared to existing methods.

This paper presents a centering theory-based framework for coreference resolution, building upon previous research. We discuss the relevance of centering theory to neural coreference resolution systems and develop a center-based approach to identifying textual cores. We then perform an experimental analysis to assess the inherent bias in modern state-of-the-art neural coreference resolution systems towards centering theory, using the OntoNotes 2.0 dataset. We also incorporate a novel metric to evaluate the systems' performance in accordance with centering theory. Our results reveal that the systems exhibit inherent bias that aligns with the principles of centering theory, and that the systems' preferred structure adheres to the theory's predictions. We provide a centering profile for each system, offering a comprehensive evaluation of their performance in relation to the principles of center-based approaches.

The spread of WiFi has made it possible to deliver data and access network services efficiently. However, determining the distance between a device and a WiFi access point is a challenging task. This paper presents a method for estimating distances between an access point and a device using supervised machine learning. The process involves collecting signal strength data at known distances, training a regression model, and using it to predict distances based on new data. The approach is validated through experiments, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method.

In energy recovery linear accelerators, beam breakup instability poses a significant challenge, particularly when dealing with regenerative patterns and high charge-to-mass ratios. These systems are prone to instability due to their inherently closed loops, leading to a wide range of possible vacuum chamber designs that can impact performance. We have evaluated four filling designs for the CLIC decelerator, utilizing a feedback model that accounts for electron cloud effects and surface resistivity in the beam pipe. Our findings reveal that filling designs with shorter beam sections exhibit less susceptibility to beam breakup, as evidenced by simulations showing a 50% increase in stable beam current compared to designs with continuous beam sections.

We have calculated the one-loop correction to the process where a quark emits two gluons, specifically in the $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. Our calculation covers the process in the Regge limit and within the broad kinematic range. Our calculation in the Regge limit matches the results of previous literature, while our calculation in the broad kinematic range is new. We obtained our calculation using the effective theory of high-energy quarks, which consists of two components: a theory of interacting gluons and a theory of free high-energy quarks. We have expressed the effective theory of high-energy quarks in terms of a Wilson line operator.

This research examines the behavior of polymer brushes with free ends that are subjected to strong stretching and have arbitrary surface configurations. The study uses self-consistent field theory to analyze these complex systems, which are composed of polymers whose ends can either be left unattached or be attached to reactive groups on the surface. The authors investigate the conditions under which unattached polymer ends are excluded from certain regions in the brush, a phenomenon known as end exclusion. The research reveals that end exclusion is a result of the strong stretching of the brush and is not influenced by the presence of reactive groups. The theory predicts that end exclusion is most pronounced in brushes with high stretching and low density, and that the location of the excluded region is determined by the distance from the surface and the position of the brush's mid-point. The research also reveals that end exclusion is more pronounced in brushes with high stretching and low density, and that the location of the excluded region is determined by the distance from the surface and the position of the brush's mid-point. The theory is validated through Monte Carlo simulations, which show that the predicted end exclusion regions are in good agreement with the simulated results. The research has implications for the design of surface coatings and for the understanding of polymer brushes in a wide range of applications.

Aim of this work is to define and examine the concept of the trimmed metric dimension within a graph. Basically, it's a variation of the metric dimension where, given any two points in the graph, we take the second smallest distance between their unique representations. We provide a method to calculate the trimmed metric dimension and examine its properties, including a relationship with the standard metric dimension. Additionally, we apply the trimmed dimension to resolve problems related to locating an object in a network when we have limited information about its possible locations.

A technique is proposed to create a comprehensive "residual map" of the entire sky by subtracting the background radiation from the one observed by the Fermi Large Area Telescope. This is achieved by leveraging a machine learning algorithm, specifically a random forest, to analyze the energy spectrum of gamma rays across various energy ranges. This method is applied to data collected between 2008 and 2017 within the 0.1-300 GeV energy spectrum. The resulting residual map reveals unaccounted radiation and provides a tool for researchers to investigate potential new discoveries. Notably, it highlights several sources with unusual behavior, including the enigmatic GJ 1245, the recently identified pulsar associated with the VHE-emitting region around TeV gamma-ray 1, and unexpected radiation patterns around the gas clouds TWA 5 and TWA 9.

To enhance the efficiency of verification protocols, we propose a new structural concept called a monochromatic set, which is a collection of functions that behave consistently under composition. We demonstrate that the class of monos, which verify type-safe function replacements, does not behave well in terms of compositional security. To address this issue, we introduce a more efficient and compositely secure class called a serial monarchy, which is a subset of monos that exhibits both closure under composition and the ability to compose their inverses. We then develop a set of verification rules and a monoidal co-sheaf functor that allows us to compose monos effectively, with serial monarchies serving as a secure alternative. We also show that this new class is capable of verifying a wide range of practical verification proofs, including those involving list operations, tree manipulations, and shuffling, with an improved proof-checking performance compared to existing methods.

We have developed a method to identify binary asteroids in Pan-STARRS1 images, utilizing their light curve characteristics. Our approach involves measuring the separation and orientation of binary asteroids through image analysis, and detecting their astrometric wobble as they orbit. By compiling a dataset of binary asteroids' orbital parameters, we can predict the wobble amplitude for a given time exposure. This prediction can be used to determine whether a specific time-delay interferometry variable (TTV) will be detectable in a specific survey. Our analysis of Pan-STARRS1 reveals that binary asteroids with an orbital semi-major axis larger than 2 arcseconds and an inclination between 10 and 70 degrees should be detectable. We have compiled a list of potential binary asteroids that may be present in the Pan-STARRS1 dataset, and these candidates can be further studied to confirm their binary nature.

This research develops an estimation and inference method for panel data within networks, specifically for identifying peer effects in a partially linear regression model. The study seeks to distinguish between genuine peer effects and spurious correlations caused by similar individuals, resulting in misleading conclusions if not properly addressed. The proposed estimator achieves a root-n rate of convergence and valid standard errors, even in scenarios where peer effects are present and rates of convergence are slower, as long as certain regularity conditions are met, which are discussed in detail. The methodology's practical application is demonstrated through the analysis of the determinants of CEO compensation, replicating and extending the findings of Acemoglu, Elder, Yagan, Li, and Tuzun (2022).

We introduce the GDM dataset, comprising 100 in-depth interviews between players and an AI Dungeon Master (DM) during a Dungeons and Dragons game. This data offers significant insights into the complex interactions and the demanding capabilities required of a DM. We analyze the data to identify areas where DMs excel, as well as challenges that a DM must navigate. We then integrate these lessons with the underlying theory of mind to develop a DM agent based on the proposed intention-driven framework. This agent demonstrates the ability to handle theory of mind and guide the game, surpassing the baseline performance. We believe the GDM dataset and associated findings provide valuable guidance for advancing conversational agents in real-world settings.

A primary focus in the study of complex protein knots is understanding how their intricate topological structures influence function and folding. While experimental and theoretical approaches have been utilized to analyze the folding dynamics of complex protein knots, a lesser-explored aspect of this issue is the effect of their intricate topological structures on their folding pathways. In this study, a random ensemble of two-state protein models with complex knots was generated, and a topological measure was developed to identify the ensemble's preferred states and potential pathways for folding. This development revealed that the ensemble's intricate topological structure constrains its state space, resulting in a preference for self-crossing-free configurations that can be characterized as "loose" or "tight" depending on their spatial arrangement. Furthermore, the study found that the ensemble's folding process follows a deterministic pathway from loose to tight configurations, which aligns with the folding process observed in native states of complex protein knots in reality.

We define symplectic mapping category groups for the blown-up tori in symplectic geometry, extending the concept of symplectic mapping category, which was previously defined for closed symplectic manifolds. We prove that this new invariant effectively distinguishes the blown-up tori from one another based on the number of times they can be further blown up while maintaining the symplectic property, providing a way to differentiate them from each other and from other divisible closed symplectic manifolds.

The implications of the latter case are explored in the context of the early universe and laboratory experiments. The connection between the unusual theorem and the breakdown of a global gauge symmetry is established, revealing that in this situation, the massless modes correspond to the physical components of the massive gauge bosons. The relationship between the unusual Nambu-Goldstone theorem and the mechanism of baryon mass generation is also examined. We present DISCO, a novel framework for enhancing underperforming utterances in natural language inference tasks. Inspired by similar techniques like knowledge distillation and hypothetical question answering, we apply the concept to the RNLI dataset, a natural language inference dataset consisting of everyday language inputs. DISCO operates in two phases: initially, it substitutes natural inputs with more complex hypothetical inputs generated by a large language model, capturing superior performance from the model. Subsequently, it refines the phrasal hypotheticals by fine-tuning a smaller version of the large language model using the dataset. We further introduce a performance improvement strategy, incorporating synthetic inputs to fine-tune the NLU model. Our experiments reveal that incorporating high-ability hypothetical inputs significantly outperforms using only the RNLI dataset, while pre-trained inputs provide a modest performance boost. Moreover, we observe that applying the concept of hypothetical question-answering to the MRDCN baseline yields substantial performance gains.

Remote epitaxy is a relatively new method for growing crystals that takes advantage of the transfer of atomic structure information through the substrate beneath a two-dimensional material. Although it has been successful in certain applications, remote epitaxy faces limitations in controlling the composition of compounds, which can hinder its potential. In this study, we introduce a new technique for preparing samples that allows for precise control of the interaction between remote epitaxy and other forms of growth, enabling researchers to tailor the bonding between a film and its substrate. By utilizing this approach, we were able to grow a complex Heusler compound, MnPtSb, on graphene grown on sapphire, which exhibited excellent quality with a low defect rate and a crystal structure that closely matched the substrate. Our findings demonstrate that the innovative sample preparation method used in this study is a powerful tool for growing intricate compounds on remote epitaxial substrates.

For a positive prime number $p$, we examine $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes and establish that their dimension must be at least $2p+1$. Furthermore, we identify the conditions under which the code's dimension equals $2p+1, 2p+2,$ or $2p+3$. The concept of a code with a zero component having a specific period is introduced, and we demonstrate that the dimension of the code's kernel is directly related to the dimensions of its zero components. The relationship between the dimensions of the code and its kernel is also explored.

Supervised learning models excel when there's an abundance of labeled data, but their effectiveness diminishes significantly in scenarios with limited labels. This limitation is particularly pronounced in applications where labels consist of a single category, as it often hinders the development of systems capable of recognizing multiple simultaneous attributes or characteristics. Such systems are crucial in a wide array of applications, including image analysis, medical diagnostics, and sentiment assessment. This research explores the potential of leveraging just one positive label per data point to train multi-label classification models, by applying advanced techniques such as self-supervised learning and data augmentation. Experiments conducted on multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach can achieve superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods, even when working with a single positive label per data point.

This research paper addresses the challenge of categorizing heart sounds into normal and abnormal classes under noisy conditions. Given the significance of heart sound analysis for diagnosing cardiac conditions, we first investigate the effects of various noise types and intensities on the S1 and S2 components of heart sounds. Our findings reveal that symmetric noise has the least impact on the detectability of S1 and S2, whereas asymmetric noise significantly reduces their detectability. Moreover, the research demonstrates that the effects of noise are more pronounced in patients with heart conditions than in healthy individuals. Building on these insights, we develop a novel, low-complexity categorization method that distinguishes between normal and abnormal heart sounds based on their responses to different noise types. Furthermore, we explore the application of convolutional neural networks for low-complexity heart sound categorization. Our results indicate that the proposed method achieves a high accuracy of 97% while maintaining a low computational cost of 100 CPU cycles per sample.

The rapid growth of wearable technology has created a significant demand for personalized healthcare applications. However, the substantial storage and privacy concerns associated with health data have hindered the development of such applications. Federated learning has emerged as a promising solution for training models in a decentralized manner while preserving data privacy. Nevertheless, the challenges of training accurate models efficiently and transferring knowledge across different wearable devices remain unresolved. To address these challenges, we present FedHealth, a federated transfer knowledge framework for wearable healthcare that enables accurate model training and seamless knowledge transfer across devices. FedHealth incorporates a novel adaptive model compression technique to optimize model performance and a knowledge transfer protocol to facilitate cross-device learning. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate FedHealth's superiority in terms of model accuracy and knowledge transfer efficiency compared to existing methods.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies that consider higher statistical properties like skewness and kurtosis in asset returns, examining the connections between various optimization-based approaches. In doing so, it highlights the limitations of popular methods, such as the CRO and CKR portfolio frameworks, and presents alternative strategies that leverage these non-Gaussian properties to improve predictive capabilities and risk assessment accuracy.

Consider a one-period financial market with two options for exiting the market at either time $s$ or $t$, with corresponding costs $s\mapsto c_s$ and $s\mapsto d_s$. These costs are right-continuous functions representing the cost of leaving the market. The goal is to determine the optimal exit time that maximizes the net proceeds. This problem is akin to a non-anticipative switching control issue. We establish the existence of a solution and derive a characterization of the optimal solution using a reflected backward stochastic differential equation with a right-continuous barrier. We also provide an application to a real option issue involving the purchase of an asset and the construction of an associated optimal stopping problem. We further explore a switching control issue with general costs, including a case where the costs are semi-markovian.

In our investigation of leptoquark pair production mechanisms, we focus on scalar leptoquarks and analyze their production via two main processes: fusion of two gluons and the interaction of a leptoquark with an incoming particle. We have determined the cross sections for these processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) for various masses and coupling constants. Our research reveals that leptoquark pair production via gluon fusion is a significant process to consider, especially at higher energies and leptoquark masses. We have also identified a specific region where both processes are highly relevant and proposed that a search for a single leptoquark should be carried out in this region.

We investigate the characteristics of star-forming galaxies, focusing on those with a specific ratio of carbon monoxide to ionized carbon line intensities. It has long been established that the C I (1-0) line line is not fully thermally excited in the molecular gas, a phenomenon we believe is a general occurrence. We propose a mathematical framework to describe the relationship between the line ratios and the physical conditions of the interstellar medium, which we found to be universally applicable across different galaxies. We discovered that the line ratios are primarily influenced by the gas density, a finding that is consistent with previous research. However, our study is unique in its broad scope, encompassing over 300 galaxies, a significant increase from earlier research that focused on individual galaxies. We found that the gas densities in these galaxies are primarily in the range of 10 to 100 cm$^{-3}$, a finding that is consistent with previous research, albeit with some discrepancies. We also observed that the line ratios are not uniformly distributed, a phenomenon we attribute to the line ratio being a robust indicator of gas density, a phenomenon that is not affected by other factors such as gas temperature or gas mass. We believe that the subthermal line ratio is a valuable tool for measuring gas densities, a finding that is particularly relevant for the upcoming JWST observations of galaxies.

In 1989, Erdős and Spencer posed an intriguing question: given a set of noisy permutations of n elements, how can we identify the original, uncorrupted permutation if it exists within a certain distance from the given set? This paper focuses on resolving this problem when the distance metric used is the Hamming distance. We demonstrate that a reconstruction is feasible when the distance exceeds n/2 + c log n, where c is a positive constant, for large n. Our approach involves a novel technique for bounding the second moment of a random variable that has a binary distribution, which may have broader applications. Our solution to the problem posed by Erdős and Spencer builds upon the log-norm inequality previously established by Alon and Friedgut.

Researchers are utilizing pulsar timing arrays to detect low-frequency gravitational waves, potentially originating from supermassive black hole binaries. While previous studies have demonstrated that pulsar signals can be accurately modeled using post-Newtonian methods for higher velocity regimes, this work aims to compare the precision of these models against more conventional approaches, specifically the "effective one-body" formalism, which is known for its high precision. By conducting this comparison, we create lookup tables to facilitate the efficient computation of post-Newtonian pulsar timing array signals, enabling swift and precise modeling of pulsar responses to binary systems.

We establish that in the ASEP generalised data sequence, the particle velocities form a stochastic process exhibiting the properties of exchange, ordering, and strong mixing. In the Bernoulli and TASEP specific cases, these velocities follow the concatenation of random walks and Brownian bridges, respectively, as proven before. This dynamic behaviour mirrors that of the particle positions.

Since the beginning of the global outbreak of the new coronavirus, known as SARS-CoV-2, researchers have developed a wide range of mathematical models to study the epidemic's dynamics. This review examines the fundamental principles behind these models, covering both compartmental approaches and more advanced methodologies, including network theory and evolutionary models. It also highlights the limitations of current methodologies and the necessity for innovative approaches to address their shortcomings.

Researchers have examined how a small number of atoms interact when a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate forms molecules through the process of association. This interaction involves three-body recombination, where three atoms come together, and has been theoretically and computationally studied using a specific model that takes into account both interatomic forces and a molecule's distinct mass and interaction properties. The study found that ignoring the molecule's characteristics can lead to significant errors in predicting how these interactions evolve over time. However, accurately modeling them allows for the prediction of a unique phenomenon where a condensate can suddenly become a mixture of atoms and molecules due to an intense loss of atoms, leading to a runaway effect. The theory has been validated through numerical simulations and can be applied to a real-world experiment involving sodium atoms.

Hierarchical data is commonly used to organize information, reflecting the structure of knowledge in human cognition. Traditional storage systems effectively support hierarchy, yet emerging DNA storage technology struggles to handle hierarchical data due to its flat data nature. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages the coding advantages of DNA storage to represent a tree structure within linear data. Our method uses a tree code to map a tree structure into a linear sequence, taking into account the constraints of DNA storage. We developed an algorithm to generate tree codes that meet DNA storage requirements, resulting in a compact representation of a tree with 100 base pairs per node. Our approach enables the efficient storage and retrieval of tree structures and their contents in DNA storage, demonstrating the potential of this technology to manage complex information systems.

Our novel approach employs a neural network to efficiently solve the shallow water equations, incorporating complex topographic features and variable bed shapes. Our method leverages a trained model to provide accurate approximations of water depth and flow velocity at a significantly reduced computational cost compared to traditional numerical methods. Our results demonstrate that our approach provides highly accurate predictions of water depth and flow velocity, even in scenarios with complex geometries and extreme flow conditions. Our analysis also reveals that our model's performance improves as the complexity of the geometries and conditions increase, providing a more robust and versatile tool for hydraulic engineering applications. Our findings also highlight the importance of considering the effects of geometries and conditions on model performance, offering valuable insights for future research and development in this field.

HDR photography aims to capture a wide range of brightness levels in an image by combining multiple images taken at different exposure settings. However, selecting the ideal exposures to minimize noise in the final HDR image is a challenging task. In this work, we develop an approach to automatically determine the best exposures for any given scene, leveraging the camera's characteristics. Our method employs a statistical model to represent the noise levels of the sensor across various exposures. By optimizing a loss function, we determine the exposures that minimize noise in the final image. We further enhance our approach by fusing images taken at the same exposure settings, which significantly improves noise estimation accuracy. We incorporate the camera's settings, such as aperture and focal length, into our model to fully utilize available data. Our algorithm is capable of determining the best exposures for both static and moving scenes. When the scene is in motion, we leverage optical flow to identify pixels with consistent movement and combine their images accordingly. Our method has been successfully applied to create an automatic HDR mode for the iPhone 6s, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world scenarios.
